title: Through the roof (Mark 2:1–12)
hookLine: four friends dig through a roof to lower a paralyzed man to Jesus

lines: A HOUSE FULL TO THE DOOR.
cards: Capernaum again, and word is out that Jesus is home. The house fills. Then the doorway.
Then the street outside. Up the lane come four men carrying a fifth on a mat. He can't walk.

They've carried him all this way, and now there's a wall of backs between them and the one person they came for. The easy thing would be to stand at the edge of that crowd, sigh, and carry him home. Tomorrow, maybe.

teach.h: A ROOF OF BEAMS AND PACKED CLAY.
teach.b: A Galilean village roof was usually flat: wooden beams, branches laid across, and a thick layer of packed clay on top. So the four climb up and start digging; Mark's Greek word means digging out a hole.
Picture it from inside. Jesus is teaching, and dirt starts falling on everyone's heads. A patch of light opens.
Then a man on a mat comes down on ropes. In the King James Bible: "they uncovered the roof where he was: and when they had broken it up, they let down the bed wherein the sick of the palsy lay."
Then a small phrase: "When Jesus saw their faith." Their faith, not only the man on the mat's. Mark notices the four on the roof, sweating, clay under their nails.
And Jesus's first words surprise everyone: "Son, thy sins be forgiven thee." Some teachers of the law think, who can forgive sins but God alone?

Jesus answers with a question: which is easier to say, your sins are forgiven, or get up and walk? Then he tells the man to pick up his mat and go home, and he does, out through the crowd that wouldn't let him in.
Christians read this in more than one way. Some hear a claim about who Jesus is, since he speaks the forgiveness the scribes say belongs to God alone.
Others hear it about friendship: someone can be carried to healing by other people's faith.

teach.h: WE NEVER SAW IT ON THIS FASHION.
teach.b: The crowd's verdict is the last line: "We never saw it on this fashion." Nobody had.

how: Many Christians pray for friends by name, and churches often keep prayer lists and send people to visit, cook for or drive those who are sick, a practice some connect with the four friends on the roof.

s: Jesus saw the faith of the man on the mat alone
Mark says "their faith": the four friends on the roof counted too.

flat village roofs were built that way, which is why they could dig through.

games.q: you're one of the four. you've carried your friend all the way here, and the house is packed to the door. what do you do?
o: wait at the edge of the crowd and hope it thins.
climb to the roof and dig a hole in it.
carry him home and try again tomorrow.
games.why: they climb up and dig through the roof, and lower him on his mat. Mark says Jesus saw their faith.

practice: Bring to mind someone who is stuck right now, sick, grieving, out of work, just flat, and the crowd between them and help: the forms, the waiting, the silence.
Ask what digging would look like: a second phone call when the first went unanswered, showing up with food instead of offering, driving them, asking again.
If you pray, carry them before God the way the four carried that mat, one corner each; if you don't, hold them in mind and choose your one stubborn thing.

wordCard.voice: Paralytic, the man on the mat, carried by four friends who dug through a roof when a crowd wouldn't let them in.

orig.note: Greek: loosened at the side, the paralyzed man. It's where English gets paralytic.
